question: The European Court of Auditors has published a report entitled ‘The EU’s support for sustainable biofuels in transport’ that analyses EU policies in that area. It found that, owing to an outdated and fragmented legal framework (the EU Biofuels Strategy dates back to 2006), the EU has no clear policy perspective on biofuels.

Only EUR 430 million from the 2014-2020 programming period and the Horizon 2020 programme were made available for research and support for biofuels. Investment in the sector has not been forthcoming as a result of EU policies, which have made it uncompetitive and unattractive to investors. In view of the above: 1.

Was the failure to draw up proper strategic plans and economic measures, a failure which has severely restricted the development of biofuels, a deliberate political choice to benefit the electricity sector?

Can an effective strategic plan for biofuels – the purpose of which, as stated in the report, is to decarbonise transport (paragraph 53) – be a viable alternative to achieve the decarbonisation of transport?
answer: EU biofuels policy over the last decade, focused on enhancing the sustainability framework for biofuels. These adjustments reflected an evolving understanding of sustainability issues, notably regarding the risk of indirect land use change associated with biofuels produced from food and feed crops.

The matter was clearly addressed by limiting the amounts of biofuels produced from food and feed crops that can be counted towards the targets for renewable energy and by gradually phasing out biofuels with high indirect land-use change risk. The policy direction shifted towards promoting advanced biofuels, renewable fuels of non-biological origin, as well as a stronger role for electrification.

The role of different policy and technology options to achieve carbon neutrality has been subject to several assessments. The results of the assessment showed that sustainable biofuels will, together with other options like green hydrogen, play an important role in the energy transition, in particular in hard to abate transport modes such as aviation and maritime.

However, relying exclusively on biofuels is not a viable option for decarbonizing the entire transport sector. The Commission believes that with the adoption of the relevant legislation, the strategic position of biofuels has been clarified.
